extracted.intended_audience: aspiring courtiers / gentlemen at a Renaissance court; readers of conduct literature
extracted.subtask_description: Prescriptive rules and situational guidance for the behaviour, deportment, accomplishments, and public presentation of a courtier so as to win praise, avoid envy, and act with grace and honour. The text gives general principles (judgment, avoidance of affectation) and many concrete examples for speech, arms, dancing and public displays.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid affectation
rubrics_metrics.description: Let him above all avoid affectation, as the Count rightly advised.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit injunction to shun artificial mannerisms; affectation is presented as the foremost failing to be guarded against. (Original phrasing: "let him above all avoid affectation")

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider the circumstances before acting or speaking
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider what thing he is doing or saying, the place where he is doing it, in whose presence, the cause that impels him, his age, his profession, the object he has in view, and the means that may conduce thereto.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These 'circumstances' determine whether a given behaviour is appropriate; examples include not fencing when others are dancing, not telling jests to a bereaved mother, and tailoring athletic display to the company present.

rubrics_metrics.name: Order one's life so all qualities form a single, consistent whole
rubrics_metrics.description: Order his whole life, and to make the most of his good qualities in intercourse with all men everywhere, without exciting envy thereby... let him order the tenor of his life in such fashion, that the whole may be in keeping with these parts and be seen to be always and in everything accordant with his own self.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for consistency so that separate virtues reinforce each other and present one coherent person; the whole life should compound the parts into one body of good qualities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use contrast and balance among qualities
rubrics_metrics.description: By means of contrast and as it were foil to the one, he must make the other more clearly seen... like good painters who display lights by use of shadow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deliberately combine opposing traits (e.g., boldness with modesty) so each enhances the other; practical examples: gentleness enhances a valiant man's boldness, modesty makes boldness seem greater.

rubrics_metrics.name: Speak little, do much; conceal praiseworthy deeds tactfully
rubrics_metrics.description: To speak little, to do much, and not to boast of praiseworthy deeds but to conceal them tactfully — enhances both these attributes in the case of one who knows how to employ this method with discretion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Boasting undermines praise; prefer quiet accomplishment and let others notice rather than self-aggrandize.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use judgment to do what is seasonable
rubrics_metrics.description: He should have good judgment… and be able to use what he knows seasonably and in a well-bred way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by examples of ridiculous out-of-season behaviour (e.g., dancing a morris-dance in the street at an inappropriate time, joking when consoling a bereaved person). Judgment about timing and propriety is central.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware hidden faults and conceit
rubrics_metrics.description: Faults are not always of the same degree: a man may refrain from public folly and yet display tiresome conceit or praise himself out of season; these faults are often covered by a veil that does not suffer them to be seen by him who commits them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Self-conceit blinds people to subtle embarrassments; precepts help reveal and correct those hidden faults.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid extremes; follow a prudent, judicious choice
rubrics_metrics.description: The right course lies in a certain prudent and judicious choice, and in discerning the more or less which all things gain or lose by being done opportunely or out of season.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moderation and discrimination in conduct trump rigid rules; apply proportionate behaviour to each situation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perform in battle and brave deeds with minimum company and before nobility
rubrics_metrics.description: When in a skirmish or action or battle, he ought to arrange discreetly to withdraw from the crowd, and to perform those glorious and brave deeds that he has to do, with as little company as he can, and in sight of all the noblest and most respected men in the army, and especially (if possible) before the very eyes of his king or of the prince whom he serves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bravery should be displayed so that honour accrues to the right observers; avoid risky or ignoble exploits that win no proper recognition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seek deserved honour; avoid false and unmerited renown
rubrics_metrics.description: It is wrong to seek false and unmerited renown, and... it is wrong also to defraud oneself of the honour that is one's due, and not to seek that praise which alone is the true reward of worthy effort.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not pursue sham glory, but also do not hide or fail to present worthy deeds so that legitimate recognition is lost.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be fully equipped and prepared before public displays of arms
rubrics_metrics.description: When our Courtier has to take part in [public bodily exercises], he must first contrive to be so well equipped in point of horses, weapons and dress, that he lacks nothing; and if he does not feel himself well provided with everything, let him on no account engage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public failure from lack of preparation is shameful; proper equipment (horse caparison, attire, mottoes, devices) is part of the performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adapt speech and conduct to the profession and sex of those present
rubrics_metrics.description: He will have regard to the profession of those with whom he converses, and will govern himself accordingly, — speaking in one way with men and in another way with women.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adjust content, tone and detail (especially about arms and martial deeds) to the audience; e.g., do not recount grisly martial details to a woman unfamiliar with them.

rubrics_metrics.name: When touching on personal credit (martial feats), do so covertly
rubrics_metrics.description: If he wishes to touch on something that is to his credit, he will do so covertly, as if by chance in passing, and with the discreetness and caution that Count Ludovico expounded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Self-promotion should be indirect and seem accidental rather than boastful; use discretion to avoid vanity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make public athletic and performative displays graceful as well as skillful
rubrics_metrics.description: In public shows — jousts, tourneys, stick-throwing, or any other bodily exercise — mindful of the place and presence in which he is, he will contrive to be not less elegant and graceful than unerring with his weapons, and to feast the spectators' eyes with all those things which he thinks may give him an added grace.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine technical proficiency with presentational elegance (horse, costume, devices); spectacle and aesthetics matter for reputation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid engaging in contests where loss is likely to bring shame (e.g., with peasants)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whoever cares to wrestle or run or leap with peasants, ought to do so as a matter of practice and out of courtesy… and a man ought to be almost sure of winning; else let him not engage, because it is too unseemly and shameful a thing, and beneath his dignity, to see a gentleman vanquished by a peasant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public losses against socially inferior opponents damage reputation; only compete when confident of victory or when the context makes condescension virtuous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practice non-professional arts discreetly and do not appear to seek praise for them
rubrics_metrics.description: The game of tennis and other sports... our Courtier should practise this, and all the others except the handling of arms, as something that is not his profession, and let him show that he does not seek or expect praise for it, nor let him seem to devote much care or time to it, although he may do it admirably.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate music, dancing, sports, etc., as graceful accomplishments but keep them subordinate to one's principal duties so as not to appear preoccupied with them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain dignity in public dancing; reserve more risque/agile steps for private
rubrics_metrics.description: When dancing in the presence of many and in a place full of people, he should preserve a certain dignity, albeit tempered with a lithe and airy grace of movement... in a room privately... he may try both [agilities] and may dance morris-dances and brawls; but not in public unless he be masked.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public choreography should fit status; more showy or rustic steps suit private or masked contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not let habitual small affectations (singing under breath, dancing through streets) reveal vanity
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not be like some men who delight in music, and in speaking with anyone always begin to sing under their breath whenever there is a pause... Others always go dancing as they pass through streets and churches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Small, recurrent self-display habits expose conceit and offend decorum; avoid mannerisms that draw attention to self outside proper occasions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time your appearance in public spectacles to gain advantage
rubrics_metrics.description: He will never be among the last to show themselves, knowing that the crowd and especially women gaze much more attentively upon the first than upon the last; for... at the start are eager for novelty and observe and are impressed by every trifle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer to present oneself early in an event when novelty attracts attention; strategic positioning can increase impact.
